source.title: HE-SNR: Uncovering Latent Logic via Entropy for Guiding Mid-Training on SWE-BENCH
source.authors: Yue-Yang Wang; Jiawei Fu; Bao-Long Bi; Xili Wang; Xiaoqing Liu

page_placements.theme: Task-aligned capability and representation proxies predict some downstream outcomes

record.tranche_reason: The study compares pretraining-loss-based metrics with downstream SWE-BENCH performance using its own evaluation setup, but does not reproduce the scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The study does not sweep parameter count, training tokens, or compute to fit scaling laws, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal allocations. It reports PPL and HE-PPL relationships with downstream performance in Figure 6; those results bear on V6. HE-SNR correlations and token-filtering ablations are reported as findings about an alternative proxy, not as evidence about scaling or pretraining loss, and are recorded under fits_no_version. Scaling-law statements in the references are not treated as results.
record.test_reason: The study compares standard PPL on held-out SWE trajectories with post-SFT SWE-bench Pass@1 across mid-training checkpoints. It argues that loss does not predict this downstream task, which bears on the loss half of V6. It fits no scaling laws, so V1–V5 and V7 are untouched.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that standard PPL weakly correlates with downstream SWE-bench performance and is distorted by the 'Long-Context Tax'. With token filtering, their HE-SNR metric shows a near-linear, rank-consistent relationship with post-SFT Pass@1. They also argue that SFT degrades prediction on high-entropy tokens, a source of the alignment tax.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a different mid-training evaluation metric and does not reproduce the original scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: The PPL-derived metric's relationship with downstream performance changes with token selection and filtering (Thought versus Action tokens, and filtering of formatting, whitespace, symbols, and comments).

fits_no_version.finding: Entropy-based proxies (HE-PPL, HE-SNR) on filtered Action tokens track post-SFT SWE-bench scores closely; HE-SNR on the full filtering pipeline gives Pearson 0.9649 and Kendall 0.9794, versus 0.5581/0.5192 on Thinking tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Entropy-thresholded, token-filtered likelihood metrics on task trajectories predict post-SFT agentic performance better than standard PPL.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The reported PPL/HE-PPL relationships in Figure 6 are not given as numerical correlations in the text. Evaluation uses two proprietary MoE model families and a curated dataset of 500 trajectories; the paper states that broader architecture and domain validation remains future work. No scaling-law or compute-optimal allocation experiment is reported.

untested.parts: Downstream predictability from scale (parameters, tokens or compute); loss on general held-out pretraining text; non-agentic benchmarks.
All: no sweep of parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small runs.
All: no shape ablation at fixed size.
All: no power-law fits in other regimes.
All: no exponent or fitting comparisons.

missing.what: PPL on filtered Action tokens versus SWE-bench Pass@1 during the 128K extension. For MoE-A26B, PPL and Top-1 accuracy degrade at Step 200 while Pass@1 improves (an 'inverse correlation'). For MoE-A3B the tax is negligible.
SFT lowers global PPL while HE-PPL and HE-SNR degrade, so loss changes need not track capability.

record.verdict_notes: The V6 evidence is narrow: two proprietary MoE families, a single agentic benchmark, and mid-training checkpoints rather than models of differing scale. The 'loss' is PPL on 500 curated SWE trajectories, not general held-out pretraining loss. The authors are affiliated with the developer of the evaluated models. No correlation numbers are given for PPL itself.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss trends in parameters, tokens, or compute, including the several-orders-of-magnitude condition.
Whether fits on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their growth with compute.
Effects of architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability from scale is not tested; the study evaluates PPL-derived metrics on its tested checkpoints and SWE-BENCH setting only.
The study does not test scaling-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, or departures from a single scaling-law curve.

relationships.condition: Standard PPL on held-out SWE Thought+Action tokens, MoE-A3B and MoE-A26B mid-training checkpoints across a 32K→128K context extension, scored by post-SFT SWE-bench-Verified Pass@1
relationships.reason: The authors state standard PPL correlates poorly with Pass@1, and one checkpoint's PPL fails to track a clear SWE gain (r1). The evidence is figure-only, and context extension is a likely confound.
relationships.display_finding: Standard perplexity correlated poorly with Pass@1 and failed to track a clear improvement at one checkpoint, although context extension likely confounded the comparison.

relation.reason: Its own checkpoint comparisons test whether evaluation loss predicts post-SFT SWE-bench-Verified Pass@1.

tranche.reason: The study directly argues and reports that standard PPL fails to track downstream SWE performance during mid-training and context extension, bearing on V6.

source_check.notes: Standard-PPL correlation is qualitative and figure-only; context extension complicates generalization beyond this setting. HE-SNR correlations concern a constructed proxy, and no power-law fit or scaling extrapolation is tested.
